paragraphs.heading: Chances that depend on what you know
paragraphs.text: Conditional probability is the chance of one event once you know, or assume, that another event has happened. Say the chance that any given person is coughing on any given day is only 5%. If you know the person is sick, coughing becomes much more likely, perhaps 75%. In symbols, P(Cough) = 5% while P(Cough|Sick) = 75%, where the bar is read as given.

paragraphs.heading: The definition
paragraphs.text: The chance of A given B is defined as the chance that both happen, divided by the chance of B. It is written P(A∣B) and equals P(A ∩ B)/P(B). When every outcome is equally likely, this is simply the share of the outcomes in B that are also in A. This formula is a definition, not merely a result derived from theory. If B has probability zero, the conditional probability is undefined.

paragraphs.heading: A dice example
paragraphs.text: Someone secretly rolls two fair six-sided dice and tells you only that the total is 5 or less. What is the chance the first die shows 2? There are 36 equally likely pairs, each with chance 1/36. Here B is the event that the sum is at most 5 and A is the event that the first die is 2, so P(A∣B) = (3/36)/(10/36) = 3/10.

paragraphs.heading: When knowing changes nothing
paragraphs.text: The conditional chance of A given B may or may not equal the plain chance of A. When P(A|B) = P(A), the events are called independent: learning about one tells you nothing new about the other. The two events also need not be related or happen at the same time.

paragraphs.heading: Direction matters
paragraphs.text: The chance of A given B usually differs from the chance of B given A. A person with dengue fever might have a 90% chance of testing positive. Yet a person who tests positive might have only a 15% chance of really having this rare disease, because false positives are common. Treating the two numbers as the same causes reasoning errors, often seen in base rate fallacies.

paragraphs.heading: Turning it around
paragraphs.text: Since information is often limited, it can help to reverse a conditional probability with Bayes' theorem, which gives P(A∣B) as P(B∣A) times P(A), divided by P(B). Another option is to lay the numbers out in a conditional probability table to show how the events relate. In the Bayesian reading, the event you condition on counts as evidence. P(A) is the chance of A before taking evidence E into account, and P(A|E) is the updated chance after it.
